paras: The Newark crowd attack on Clarence Spain and Mary Stein took place in Newark, New Jersey, in early August 1905, when a street crowd set upon a Black man and his white bride as they left the justice of the peace's office where they had just married. No injuries were reported and the couple got away, but papers in New York and Denver carried the story.

Spain, 28, was described as a Black man from Bloomfield, called "dapper" by the Evening World and "well-educated" by the Jewish Outlook of Denver. Stein, 23, worked as a maid for a family on Douglas Road in Glen Ridge, and the Denver paper described her as "a pretty Jewess." According to the Evening World, a Justice Bassett married them on the night of August 3, while the Jewish Outlook said a Justice Henry Bosset performed the ceremony on a "Friday night" in Justice Miller's law office at Plane and Market streets.

As the couple were about to board a trolley car, someone spread word that they were bride and groom, and a crowd quickly gathered. In the Evening World's account the crowd jostled them, shouted, and "several times almost knocked them down," then leered at them as they boarded the car. The Denver item said instead that "an attempt was made to attack the negro" and that the couple evaded the crowd, but its text breaks off before explaining how. Neither account reports arrests.

The Evening World ran the story first, on August 4, under a Newark dateline, describing an "unpleasant reception" and a couple "Roughly Treated" by a "Street Throng." Two weeks later the Jewish Outlook printed a longer version among its community notes, calling it an "unusual marriage" and putting the bride's Jewish identity first. Neither paper commented on the crowd's conduct, and no Black-press account appears in the coverage.

The accounts differ on the night of the wedding, on the justice's name and office, and on whether the crowd jostled both of them or tried to attack Spain alone; the Evening World's is the earlier, dated dispatch.

reader.title: Newark crowd attack on Clarence Spain and Mary Stein
bases: A street crowd jostled, shouted at and nearly knocked down a newly married Black man and his white bride (A1), or attempted to attack him before the couple evaded it (A4); no injury is reported.

Two reports with different details and wording (A1 names Justice Bassett and a trolley car; A4 names Justice Miller's office at Plane and Market streets and Richfield Road) agree that a crowd set upon the couple as they left the justice's office after the wedding.
